articles.title: Watch: Woman with mental health history charges at NYPD officers with kitchen knives before being shot
articles.summary: US News: A woman who stabbed two people in New York City's Times Square before being shot by police charged at officers wielding two kitchen knives and refused.
articles.body: A woman who stabbed two people in New York City's Times Square before being shot by police charged at officers wielding two kitchen knives and refused repeated demands to surrender, authorities said. The investigators ruled out any immediate indication that the attack was terrorism-related.The 49-year-old Queens woman was confronted by NYPD officers shortly after stabbing a 32-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man on Monday afternoon. The younger woman died from her injuries, while the man remained in stable condition.The dramatic confrontation unfolded near an NYPD substation outside One Times Square, where officers spent several minutes attempting to persuade the woman to put down the weapons, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said.The woman instead told officers, “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” Tisch said.Police then used a Taser, but it failed to incapacitate her. Video recorded by bystanders showed the woman subsequently moving towards the officers while waving the knives.Two officers opened fire, striking the woman. She fell to the ground and was handcuffed by police, while officers administered first aid. She was later pronounced dead.Despite the apparently random nature of the attack and the violent confrontation that followed, police said there was no evidence to suggest that the incident was a terrorist attack.Tisch said the woman had a “documented mental health history with the NYPD”, including incidents in 2018 and 2019. She did not have an arrest history with the department, and police have not disclosed further details about her mental health history.The attack began when the woman pulled two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed the 68-year-old man in the abdomen as he waited to cross the street with his wife after emerging from a subway station. Seconds later, she stabbed the 32-year-old woman, also in the abdomen.Both victims were taken to hospital. Police have not identified them as authorities continue to notify their relatives.“This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said.NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers who confronted the woman, saying their actions helped prevent the situation from escalating further in one of the city's busiest tourist areas.“We know that those families’ lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment," Mamdani said.Police temporarily shut part of 7th Avenue and urged the public to stay away from the area as investigators examined the scene.The incident came as violent crime continues to decline across New York City. Homicides are down 24% so far this year and are on course to potentially reach their lowest level in decades.It was, however, the second fatal stabbing in Times Square this year. articles.title: Three new rooms, wall paintings found at Smyrna in Izmir as archaeologists trace a 2,000-year-old Roman water channel
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The ancient city of Smyrna in Izmir has revealed new clues about how the city changed during Late Antiquity. Excavations at the Smyrna Agora have unco.
articles.body: The ancient city of Smyrna in Izmir has revealed new clues about how the city changed during Late Antiquity. Excavations at the Smyrna Agora have uncovered three previously unidentified rooms dating to the 5th and 6th centuries AD. Two of the rooms contained mosaic floors while the third had a marble floor. Archaeologists also found wall paintings around the Agora and the Theatre of Smyrna that had not been recorded before.According to Anadolu Ajansı (Turkish news agency), the three newly identified rooms and previously unseen wall paintings have helped archaeologists trace around 150 metres of an ancient Roman water channel. The channel is believed to have carried water continuously for nearly 2,000 years, although its source has not been identified yet. Researchers are now investigating where the water came from and how the system supplied the ancient city.What did archaeologists discover inside the three new rooms in Smyrna Agora, TurkeyExcavations at the Smyrna Agora have uncovered three previously unidentified rooms that extend from a mosaic floor discovered last year. Two of the rooms feature mosaic floors, while the third has a marble floor. Archaeologists have dated the structures to the 5th and 6th centuries AD, which places them in the Late Antiquity period. Prof. Dr. Akın Ersoy, head of the excavation, said the newly discovered structures share similarities with the Hillside Houses at the ancient city of Ephesus.The excavation has also revealed previously unseen wall paintings around the Smyrna Agora and the Theatre of Smyrna. Ersoy said, "This is the first time we've encountered murals in these locations. We had never come across them before in the Smyrna Agora or around the theater." The paintings offer new clues about the appearance and use of these parts of the ancient city during Late Antiquity.Why are these discoveries important to Smyrna's historyThe discoveries come from a period when cities across the Roman world were undergoing significant changes. Smyrna was changing during the same period, and the newly uncovered structures offer archaeological evidence of that transformation. Ersoy said the three rooms share characteristics with the Hillside Houses at Ephesus, raising the possibility that they may have served a public function. The previously undocumented wall paintings from the Agora and theatre areas add further clues about the city's changing appearance.What does the 150-metre Roman water channel revealThe excavation has also shed light on Smyrna's ancient water system, with archaeologists tracing around 150 metres of a Roman-era water channel. Its source has yet to be identified, and the team is now working to determine where the channel began. Ersoy explained that Smyrna's water needs during the Roman period were met through canals linked to springs. One possible source may have been a spring near the Namazgah Bath and Kurşunlu Mosque, south of the Agora. The water may have travelled towards the Smyrna Agora along the traced route. Researchers believe the channel could have carried water continuously for nearly 2,000 years.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Top tech investor Gavin Baker regrets his comments on data centres; says what I should have said is: There are reasonable concerns and ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Top tech investor Gavin Baker has publicly expressed regret over his earlier remakes dismissing opposition to data centers. In a post last week, Baker.
articles.body: Top tech investor Gavin Baker has publicly expressed regret over his earlier remakes dismissing opposition to data centers. In a post last week, Baker had written that ‘any politician opposed to data centers is unqualified to hold public office’, calling them a godsend for blue-collar workers and small towns. However, now Baker struck a a different tone, saying he regretted the phrasing and acknowledged that there were “reasonable concerns” about data centers around 18 months ago.Gavin Baker’s original post on data centersBaker's earlier post declared that "nature is healing" on the data center debate, going as far as saying any politician opposed to data centers was unqualified to hold public office. In that post, he argued data centers were revitalizing small towns across America, delivering major benefits to blue-collar workers, lowering electricity costs, accelerating the shift to sustainable energy, and using only negligible amounts of water.The walkbackIn a follow-up post, Baker said he regretted the tone of his prior comments, offering a more measured version of his argument instead. He acknowledged that concerns about data centers were reasonable roughly 18 months ago, spanning issues like water usage, taxes, job creation, electricity prices, environmental impact, and effects on small towns. His revised position is that well-structured data center projects have since largely addressed those concerns, and that the industry's overall record now deserves to be seen as a positive for the country.Addressing key issuesBaker outlined how well-structured projects have since addressed worries over water usage, taxes, jobs, electricity prices, and environmental impact:•Water: U.S. data centers use far less water than golf courses, with newer facilities adopting closed-loop or recycled systems.•Taxes: While sales-tax exemptions drew criticism, Baker noted that property taxes from data centers have become a major revenue source in counties like Loudoun, VA and Quincy, WA.•Jobs: Demand for electricians, plumbers, welders, and HVAC technicians has surged, with unions now backing data center projects.•Power: Ratepayer-protection deals and large-load tariffs ensure households aren’t burdened by higher electricity costs. In some states, utilities have cut or frozen residential rates due to data center investments.•Environment: Facilities increasingly rely on natural gas, solar, and batteries, with commitments to carbon neutrality. Batteries also support grid stability, as seen in Texas.Impact on small townsBaker highlighted the transformation of towns like Quincy, WA, where poverty fell from 29% to 6% and tax revenues funded schools, hospitals, and libraries. He argued that data centers are “reindustrializing parts of America” and creating durable working-class jobs.A revised stanceConcluding his post, Baker said: “When the facts change, I change my mind. I hope that reasonable people who had good faith reasons to oppose data centers at least consider updating their beliefs given the change in the facts over the last 18 months.” He added that future projects should also focus on aesthetics, suggesting data centers be designed as beautifully as Grand Central Station.Read Gavin Baker’s complete post hereRegret the tone of my post on data centers yesterday.What I should have said:There were reasonable concerns about data centers 18ish months ago: water, taxes, jobs, electricity prices, the environment and what they would do to small towns. Well-structured data center projects have largely addressed these concerns today and we should be celebrating this. On balance, data centers are awesome for America in every way.On water: U.S. data centers use a fraction of what golf courses use. A lot of the numbers from 18 months ago were off by over 1000x. Newer data centers use closed-loop systems or recycled water. Should be required by every town approving a data center project.On taxes: looking only at sales-tax exemptions, as Ronan Farrow did, is the wrong way to evaluate this. Data centers pay significant property taxes. Loudoun County, which is the wealthiest county in America, now collects on the order of $1 billion a year from data centers. In Quincy, WA, data centers are more than half the property-tax roll. Over time, property taxes can go to zero while government spending increases in these towns.On jobs: this has been unambiguously awesome for blue collar Americans. Demand for electricians, plumbers, welders, HVAC techs, and contractors has gone vertical, and it is not a one-time construction job. These buildings get upgraded and expanded over time. That is why the building trades are fighting for them, and why some unions are now treating opposition to data centers as a reason not to endorse politicians.On power: the original fear was that households would pay for the incremental electricity demand in the form of higher prices. That is why the ratepayer-protection deals and the new large-load tariffs exist. The right structure is: the data center brings or pays for new generation and signs a contract long enough that existing customers are protected. Where that is happening, utilities are cutting or freezing residential rates and saying so on the record. Where it is not, people are right to object. Electricity prices are going down *today* in a number of large states because of data centers. On the environment: data centers overwhelming use natural gas today, which is the cleanest power source outside of nuclear, solar and wind. And the companies that are building the data centers are committed to carbon neutrality such that an equivalent amount of solar will likely be built. Maybe more importantly, the data centers need batteries to function effectively and these batteries can also sell energy back into the grid (which recently prevented blackouts in Texas). Over time, data centers will run on solar plus batteries.On the towns: Poverty in Quincy, WA fell from 29% to 6%. Data center taxes paid for a new high school, a hospital, a library, police and fire stations. This is happening in many left for dead former mill and farm towns that had no other bidder for the land.Data centers are actually reindustrializing parts of America and creating the kind of working-class jobs both parties have spent decades claiming to support. That should not be a partisan issue. Data centers can and should be awesome for America and they increasingly, overwhelmingly are. Supporting the outsourcing of data centers to China will likely age just as well as support for the outsourcing of high quality, blue collar manufacturing jobs to China has aged.When the facts change, I change my mind. I hope that reasonable people who had good faith reasons to oppose data centers at least consider updating their beliefs given the change in the facts over the last 18 months. This really matters for America.I will say I also think the idea of making data centers beautiful is a good one that has yet to be implemented. Data centers should be just as beautiful as Grand Central Station. We can learn a lot from the railroad buildout. Neoclassical revival ftw.Might write up open-weight AI tomorrow as this is equally essential to America.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Indian among 12 killed after Russia launches massive strike on Ukraine
articles.summary: Europe News: At least 12 people, including an Indian, were killed after Russia launched a massive aerial assault across Ukraine overnight, Ukrainian authorities sa.
articles.body: At least 12 people, including an Indian, were killed after Russia launched a massive aerial assault across Ukraine overnight, Ukrainian authorities said on Tuesday. More than a dozen people were also wounded, including three children.The attack, which began at around 6pm on Monday, involved ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, along with 218 drones and decoys, according to Ukraine’s air force. Around a third of the drones were reportedly jet-powered.The Kyiv and Odesa regions were the main targets of the assault, which marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were damaged in several areas. “Overall, 12 people were killed, among them an Indian citizen, and dozens more were injured in the attack.”Zelenskyy said seven people were killed in a strike on a railway depot in Kyiv, while authorities reported another death in the city’s Holosiivskyi district after a non-residential building was hit and caught fire. A drone also struck a residential building in the Solomianskyi district, where emergency workers rescued a man and freed a woman trapped under rubble.In the wider Kyiv region, three people were killed and 12 wounded. In Boryspil, several buildings and vehicles were damaged, while emergency crews evacuated 48 people and rescued two people from beneath the rubble.Odesa also came under heavy attack, with residential buildings and civilian infrastructure damaged. A sewing factory caught fire, while Russian forces also struck the Orlivka international ferry crossing on the border with Romania.Ukraine’s air force said its forces destroyed or suppressed 199 aerial targets, including five ballistic missiles and 187 drones. Missile and drone strikes were recorded at 28 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at another 10 sites.Zelenskyy said the attacks showed the need for stronger air defences, adding: “Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defense capabilities are insufficient.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Archaeologists discover evidence of an ancient “brand” 3,000 years before modern marketing
articles.summary: Rest of World News: More than 3,000 years ago, potters working in the desert oasis of Qurayyah in what is now northwestern Saudi Arabia were producing a distinctive paint.
articles.body: More than 3,000 years ago, potters working in the desert oasis of Qurayyah in what is now northwestern Saudi Arabia were producing a distinctive painted pottery that eventually travelled beyond the settlement where it was made. A new study titled Creating a brand. Genesis, transformation and diffusion of Qurayyah Painted Ware, published in PLOS ONE, has now combined archaeological, petrographic and chemical evidence to reconstruct how that pottery developed over several centuries, eventually becoming what researchers describe as an early example of brand-making. Known as Qurayyah Painted Ware, or QPW, the pottery was recognisable for its distinctive bichrome designs and consistent manufacturing traditions. By the time the fourth major production phase, known as QPW 4, emerged during the Late Bronze Age, the vessels were being produced in substantial quantities and had begun appearing outside Qurayyah, including at Tell el-Kheleifeh in southern Jordan and at the Hathor Shrine in Timna. Researchers argue that QPW 4 was more than simply a recognisable style of pottery: its consistent appearance, local production, export circulation and eventual imitation elsewhere suggest that people had begun associating the distinctive vessels with a particular place, quality and identity.How pottery made in the Saudi desert became recognisable across the regionThe story begins at Qurayyah, an oasis in northwestern Arabia that became the centre of a long-running pottery tradition. According to the new study, the earliest forms of Qurayyah Painted Ware, QPW 1 and QPW 2, emerged during the late Middle Bronze Age and early Late Bronze Age. The researchers found that these early productions were locally developed rather than simply copied from pottery traditions elsewhere. Over time, the production changed. Different generations of potters modified the shapes, decoration and manufacturing methods, but the basic connection to Qurayyah remained. The researchers identified seven different QPW assemblages extending from the Bronze Age into the Iron Age, showing that the painted pottery tradition continued for more than a millennium. The fourth phase, QPW 4, is where the researchers believe something different happened. By this point, the pottery had developed a particularly distinctive visual identity, while the use of local raw materials and established production techniques remained consistent. Kilns at Qurayyah also provide evidence of centralised production, including manufacturing waste and overfired vessels.For the researchers, that combination is important because a brand is not simply an attractive design. It also involves a recognisable identity tied to production, consistency and a relationship between producers and consumers. QPW 4 increasingly met those conditions.How scientists proved that some of the pottery travelled north from QurayyahThe strongest evidence for QPW 4 becoming an export product comes from pottery fragments found outside Qurayyah itself. Researchers examined samples from Tell el-Kheleifeh, a site in southern Jordan located about 130 kilometres northwest of Qurayyah. Several of the fragments had previously been identified as pottery resembling the Hejazi tradition, but the new chemical and petrographic analysis provided a more precise connection to Qurayyah. Three QPW 4-like sherds from Tell el-Kheleifeh matched Qurayyah's chemical group V032. Their mineral composition and manufacturing characteristics were also compatible with the production evidence from the Qurayyah kiln. Taken together, the researchers say the evidence strongly suggests that these vessels were actually produced at Qurayyah and then transported north to Tell el-Kheleifeh.The researchers found another important connection farther north at the Hathor Shrine in Timna, in what is now southern Israel. Two pottery sherds from the shrine also matched the same Qurayyah geochemical group. The study therefore identifies Timna, alongside Tell el-Kheleifeh, as another place where vessels produced at Qurayyah were used. The distances are significant, but the researchers are cautious about how widely they extend the conclusion. They do not claim that every piece of pottery resembling QPW 4 found throughout the Southern Levant must have been imported from Qurayyah. Chemical compatibility has so far been established only for a limited number of samples, and the authors acknowledge evidence for local production imitating the distinctive Qurayyah style elsewhere.Why researchers think QPW 4 qualifies as an ancient brandThe study's central argument is that QPW 4 meets several characteristics that researchers associate with branding. First was its appearance. The pottery developed a standardised and conspicuous visual identity, making it recognisable even outside the place where it was manufactured. Then came consistency. The researchers found evidence for continued use of local raw materials and manufacturing traditions, linking the later QPW 4 production to the earlier QPW tradition at Qurayyah. That technological continuity helped create a product that remained recognisable while still evolving over time.There is also evidence that the pottery was produced beyond what would have been required simply for local household use. Hundreds of decorated QPW 4 vessels are known, and the researchers argue that their scale of production points toward intentional commercial manufacture. Finally, there is evidence that the style was copied elsewhere. The researchers point to local imitations of QPW 4 in parts of the Southern Levant, suggesting that the pottery's visual identity had become desirable enough for other producers to reproduce it. In modern terms, that would be an important sign that the original product had developed a reputation that extended beyond its place of manufacture. The researchers therefore argue that by the final Late Bronze Age, Qurayyah's pottery tradition had developed into something resembling a recognisable regional brand, with its identity tied closely to its place of origin.What the pottery reveals about trade and identity in ancient ArabiaThe findings also challenge the idea that long-distance trade and recognisable commercial identities are primarily features of much later economies. The people producing QPW 4 were operating thousands of years before modern companies, trademarks or formal advertising existed, yet the pottery appears to have developed many of the characteristics associated with a recognisable commercial product. That does not mean ancient consumers understood the pottery as a "brand" in the modern corporate sense. The researchers use the term as an analytical framework for describing how a product can communicate information about its origin, quality, status and cultural meaning. In the case of QPW 4, its distinctive appearance and connection to Qurayyah may have helped consumers recognise and value it beyond the oasis where it was made. The researchers also point to the pottery's use in contexts that went beyond ordinary utility, including burial gifts and miniature vessels. Its visual motifs also appear to have influenced other forms of craft production, suggesting that the style had acquired a cultural identity extending beyond pottery itself.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1991, a private buyer turned 63.5-acre Cousine Island into a Seychelles nature reserve; monitoring has since recorded more than 900 nesting hawksbill turtles
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Cousine Island is a small granite island in the Seychelles, which was purchased by its current owner in 1991, after which conservation work began to p.
articles.body: Cousine Island is a small granite island in the Seychelles, which was purchased by its current owner in 1991, after which conservation work began to protect its nesting hawksbill turtles. The island covers 25.7 hectares, or about 63.5 acres, and has since developed a long-running turtle monitoring programme. Researchers and conservation staff have recorded more than 900 individual hawksbill females there since monitoring began during the 1993-94 nesting season.The figures make Cousine different from its nearby namesake, Cousin Island, which became a nature reserve in 1968 and is managed by Nature Seychelles. Cousine remains privately owned and describes itself as a private conservation sanctuary. Its conservation programme has focused on restoring native vegetation, removing introduced species and protecting endangered wildlife.The island changed hands in 1991The island's current history records that the new owners started restoration work in 1992, removing farm animals and Casuarina trees before planting indigenous and endemic species. The island says about 8,000 indigenous and endemic trees have been planted since the restoration began.A scientific study published in Conservation Science and Practice describes Cousine as a globally important hawksbill rookery and records a long-standing monitoring and management programme dating from 1991. The island has one main nesting beach, about 900 metres long, along its eastern coast.The beach is exposed to the seasonal northwest monsoon, which affects the movement of sand along the shoreline. That creates a practical problem for turtle nests, which is, areas that appear suitable when eggs are laid can later be exposed to erosion or flooding.Monitoring began with individual turtlesConservation staff identify nesting females, record their tag numbers and collect information on their nesting activity. The programme also tracks exploratory crawls, including cases where a turtle comes ashore but does not lay eggs. The International Ocean-Indian Ocean South-East Asia Marine Turtle Memorandum of Understanding, known as IOSEA, reports that Cousine recorded more than 900 individual hawksbill females between the 1993-94 nesting season and the time of its report. It also says patrols have become more intensive, with hourly beach monitoring and data collection on females and turtle tracks. The long record allows conservationists to distinguish between newly tagged turtles and females that return to the island, which also provides information on how often individual turtles nest, where they lay their eggs, and how successful those nests are.The beach itself can threaten the nestsCousine's shoreline shifts during the year as sand moves along the coast, and IOSEA reports that conservation staff began monitoring spring high and low tide marks in 2003. They used the measurements to create a beach-movement map that helps determine whether individual nests are likely to remain safe or need to be relocated.Ghost crabs present another problem, since they can prey on eggs and hatchlings, particularly in areas where their populations are concentrated. A study of Cousine's nesting beach found that the island's roughly 900-metre beach supports about 70 to 130 hawksbill nests in a typical season and that erosion and crab predation can threaten nests. Conservation workers have therefore used both beach-movement data and information about crab densities when deciding whether nests should be moved.Thousands of hatchlings reach the seaDuring the 2019-20 season, IOSEA reported that 19,089 hawksbill eggs were recorded on Cousine and 14,865 hatchlings were successfully released into the sea. Relocating a nest can protect eggs from erosion or flooding, but moving eggs can itself affect hatching outcomes. Research on Cousine's management programme has examined the use of a hatchery alongside natural incubation, with relocation reserved for clutches considered at risk.Hawksbill turtles remain listed as critically endangered, and Seychelles is one of the world's important remaining nesting areas for the species. Cousine's long-term records have given conservationists a way to follow individual females and measure changes in nesting activity rather than relying on occasional sightings. The island remains privately owned, with conservation and tourism operating alongside one another. Its current conservation programme continues to monitor nesting females and hatchlings while managing the beach conditions that determine whether their nests survive.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India eyes drones that helicopters can launch, control and send 80km into enemy territory
articles.summary: International News: Helicopter-launched loitering munitions are quickly becoming the next big frontier in aerial warfare, and recent trials are showing just how far the c.
articles.body: Helicopter-launched loitering munitions are quickly becoming the next big frontier in aerial warfare, and recent trials are showing just how far the concept has come. At Project Convergence Capstone 6, a US Army H-60M Black Hawk crew successfully executed a rocket-powered launch of the Altius-700, deploying a hunter-killer team that autonomously located a target, shared data across the formation, and carried out a strike, all without putting the helicopter crew in harm's way. It marks another meaningful step toward fielding what the US Army calls launched effects, pushing sensors and weapons deeper into contested airspace while keeping manned aircraft further back from danger.Israel, too, has been busy on this front, a private firm in has developed a modular aerial launch system that lets both utility and attack helicopters deploy its Hero-120 loitering munition. What makes the system particularly versatile is its ability to hand over control of the munition mid-flight to ground forces, enabling beyond-line-of-sight engagements and tighter coordination between air and land units. Swappable warheads mean the same platform can switch between hitting armour, soft targets, or simply conducting surveillance, all decided on the fly.India is now moving to build a similar capability of its own. The Indian Air Force is seeking Non-Line-of-Sight guided ammunition for its helicopters, aiming for a lightweight, cost-effective system with a range of 50 to 60 kilometres that can hit both armour and softer targets with real-time video feed and man-in-the-loop control, allowing crews to alter or abort a strike mid-flight if needed. Alongside this, the IAF has released a Request for Proposal for drones deployable from helicopters, expected to carry at least a 500-gram warhead over an 80 km range, and a separate Request for Information for loitering munitions launched from transport aircraft, which would need a far longer 500 km range, a 30 kg warhead, and cruising speeds of 350-400 km/h.The strategic logic here is fairly straightforward. By spreading strike and surveillance capability across helicopters, the IAF could free up its fighter fleet for other missions, a meaningful advantage given the force's ongoing squadron shortage. These air-deployable systems aren't limited to strikes either, they can just as easily be used for electronic warfare, decoy operations, or to search for targets.India isn't alone in this pursuit, the US Air Force's parallel Gremlins programme and the broader Air Launched Effects initiative both envision networked drone swarms capable of overwhelming enemy defences from range, while China, Russia and the United Kingdom are reportedly pursuing comparable concepts of their own, suggesting helicopter and transport-aircraft-launched munitions could soon become a standard fixture of modern air combat doctrine.

articles.title: In 1990, John and Karen Lewis bought 1,000 acres of Costa Rican rainforest to stop it being logged; the reserve now shelters monkeys, sloths and over 300 bird species
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the inspiring journey of John and Karen Lewis, who transformed 1,000 acres of Costa Rican rainforest into a thriving nature reserve that protects endangered species and benefits local communities.
articles.body: In 1990, John and Karen Lewis walked away from their old life in Minnesota to buy a stretch of virgin rainforest on Costa Rica's remote Osa Peninsula. What began as a two-week birdwatching trip became a decision that shaped the rest of their working lives. The couple sold nearly everything they owned to fund the purchase of roughly 1,000 acres of old-growth forest on the peninsula's southern tip, a spot so isolated that government officials warned almost nobody would ever visit it. That warning turned out to be wrong, and the land they saved is now a conservation success story.From volunteers to landownersJohn and Karen had met years earlier while serving with the US Peace Corps in Kenya, an experience that shaped their thinking about conservation and community-based tourism long before either of them had heard of the Osa. When that birdwatching trip brought them to the Osa in 1990, they were not looking for a business opportunity so much as a piece of forest large enough to matter. The lodge they eventually built there, Lapa Rios, now describes on its own website how the surrounding reserve shelters endangered monkeys, sloths and more than 300 bird species. Building a small lodge to fund the reserve's upkeep was almost an afterthought, a way to make the conservation pay for itself rather than an end in its own right.Turning a patch of jungle into a functioning nature reserve was not simple, and the Lewises spent years figuring out how to do it without displacing nearby residents. They built a school for the local community before adding tourist facilities, reflecting their belief that conservation lasts only if nearby residents benefit too. Locals were trained as lodge staff and nature guides rather than treated as an afterthought, and some of the children who first attended that school later took on roles helping to run the property.A refuge crowded with wildlifeThe reserve succeeded in ways the Lewises could not have fully predicted when they first signed the papers. As the surrounding region lost forest cover to cattle ranching and logging through the 1990s, the reserve they had quietly assembled became an increasingly important buffer for the neighbouring Corcovado National Park, itself regarded as one of the most biologically intense places on earth. Cayuga Collection, which later took over managing the lodge for the Lewises, notes that the Osa Peninsula holds all four of Costa Rica's monkey species, along with tapirs, anteaters and a wide range of frogs and snakes. The reserve serves as a corridor, allowing animals to move between protected areas that would otherwise be separated by farmland.Of the roughly 1,000 acres the Lewises bought, only a small fraction was ever cleared for the lodge, a handful of guest cottages and a footpath network, all deliberately clustered on a single ridge overlooking the Golfo Dulce. The remaining forest was left standing. That restraint is part of why the reserve still supports such a wide range of species decades after it was first established, even as tourism around it has grown considerably.Making the protection permanentBy the late 1990s, John and Karen had begun to worry about what would happen to the reserve once they were no longer around to protect it personally. They gathered experts from around the world for a week-long workshop to solve that problem, and the result was a plan to hand management to outside specialists while placing the forest under a legal arrangement no future owner could undo. In 2013, working with The Nature Conservancy and the Costa Rican legal group CEDARENA, they signed a conservation easement that binds the property in perpetuity, meaning the forest stays protected no matter who runs the lodge business housed within it, as reported at the time by Green Lodging News. That agreement completed a project that had taken more than two decades to finish. What started as a conservation project by two former aid workers has become a permanent fixture on the Osa Peninsula, one that will keep sheltering its resident sloths and monkeys long after the people who first thought to protect them are gone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'This is real': Pete Hegseth appears to mock Canadian military woman amid US-Canada tensions
articles.summary: US News: US secretary of war Pete Hegseth appeared to mock the appearance of a uniformed woman featured in a Canadian cadet post on Tuesday, sharing her image .
articles.body: US secretary of war Pete Hegseth appeared to mock the appearance of a uniformed woman featured in a Canadian cadet post on Tuesday, sharing her image on X with a Canadian flag and the words: “(this is real)”.The image, originally posted by the cadets.vernon Instagram account, showed the woman in Canadian military camouflage standing alongside another person in cadet attire. Hegseth did not explain what he meant or make any explicit reference to her weight. However, the post was widely interpreted as a weight-related jibe given his repeated use of the phrase “fit not fat” while pushing tougher physical standards in the US military.Canada’s Cadet Instructors Cadre is part of the Canadian Armed Forces Reserve. It comprises approximately 7,800 commissioned officers whose primary responsibility is the safety, supervision, administration and training of more than 52,000 cadets, according to Canada’s Department of National Defence.Hegseth has repeatedly used ‘fit not fat’Weight and physical fitness have been recurring themes in Hegseth’s push for tougher standards in the US military.At the US Army War College in April 2025, he told military leaders they needed to be “fit not fat, sharp not shabby” while discussing a force-wide review of fitness, training and physical standards.His language became more pointed at a gathering of senior US military commanders at Quantico in September 2025.“It’s completely unacceptable to see fat generals and admirals in the halls of the Pentagon,” Hegseth said while laying out stricter fitness and appearance standards. In the same speech, he also complained about seeing “fat troops” in military formations. The Pentagon subsequently issued new guidance on physical fitness and grooming standards.The language continued into 2026. In February, Hegseth praised the US Army on X by writing: “Well done @USArmy. Merit-based & Fit NOT Fat.”At West Point in May, he told graduating cadets: “You're fit, not fat. You are disciplined, not distracted.”Hegseth’s post about the Canadian cadet programme also comes at a particularly sensitive moment in relations between Washington and Ottawa, with the two neighbours locked in an escalating trade dispute and tensions rising over Canadian sovereignty.Trade talks collapse, tariffs riseTrade negotiations broke down in late August after Canada rejected last-minute US terms and suspended the talks. The United States subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on C$27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods.The Trump administration has accused Canadian policies of discriminating against US businesses, including in sectors such as motor vehicles and dairy, and imposed the duties under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.Canada disputes Washington’s case. Prime Minister Mark Carney said last-minute changes to the US proposal were “unfair, uneconomic” and called into question the reliability of any agreement. He said Ottawa would not accept terms that undermined Canadian interests and sovereignty.Among the sticking points were automobiles and broader questions over Canada’s ability to make independent decisions on trade and domestic policy.Canada targets more than 700 US productsFrom September 8, Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs of 15%, 25% and 50% on C$27.6 billion worth of US imports.The measures cover hundreds of American products and include sectors such as steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics. Ottawa says the countermeasures will match the US tariffs dollar for dollar.The stakes are considerable. The United States and Canada traded nearly $880 billion worth of goods and services in 2025, while about 72% of Canadian goods exports went to the US.The two economies are particularly closely integrated in sectors such as automobiles, where vehicles and components routinely move across the border during the manufacturing process.Carney has also pushed to reduce Canada’s dependence on the US market by expanding trade relationships elsewhere.Trump rhetoric raises sovereignty tensionsTrade is only one source of friction. Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada could become the 51st US state, remarks rejected by Canadian leaders and which have added a sovereignty dimension to the economic confrontation.The rhetoric took another turn on August 27, when Trump signed an executive order directing the US government to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”.The order directs the US interior secretary and Board on Geographic Names to update federal references to the lake. The change applies to US federal usage and does not determine what Canada or international bodies call it.Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are due to take effect on September 8, with trade negotiations between the two countries still suspended.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Florida clock survived nearly a century outdoors; one clockmaker has now spent about 700 hours restoring its 95-year-old hands, dial and metalwork
articles.summary: US News: For nearly a century, a four-faced clock stood over a busy corner in downtown Clearwater, Florida, quietly marking the passing hours as the city aroun.
articles.body: For nearly a century, a four-faced clock stood over a busy corner in downtown Clearwater, Florida, quietly marking the passing hours as the city around it changed. Years of Florida weather eventually left their mark on the historic timepiece, but instead of letting it disappear with age, a clockmaker took it apart piece by piece and spent roughly 700 hours bringing it back to life. The historic Peoples Bank clock, also known as the four-faced McClintock clock, has now returned to Cleveland Street after months of painstaking restoration. At the centre of the project was master horologist and second-generation clockmaker David H. Boyd, whose family has been working with clocks for generations. According to the Cleveland Street Alliance, Boyd and his team spent five to six months restoring the landmark, putting approximately 700 hours into preserving its original dial, hands and metalwork while adding modern GPS-regulated clockworks.A clock built for another eraThe clock had watched over Cleveland Street for generations. By the time it reached Boyd Clocks in Tampa, however, nearly a century of exposure to Florida weather had taken a toll on its components. The restoration required the clock to be dismantled rather than simply repaired in place. Its heavy steel frame was taken apart, while its copper roof, original dial and hands were removed and examined separately. Among the most important pieces were the original clock hands. According to the Cleveland Street Alliance, Boyd pointed out that the hands were still the originals and were approximately 95 years old. Rather than replacing these historic elements with new replicas, Boyd and his team restored them so that they could continue to form part of the clock's original appearance.700 hours of restorationThe project ultimately required approximately 700 hours of work. That time was spent restoring the clock's original components while also making it capable of functioning reliably in the present day. The team preserved the original dial and hands and restored the clock's metalwork. New stained-glass panels were also created, adding another layer of craftsmanship to the restoration.But preserving a historic clock does not necessarily mean leaving every part untouched. Behind its restored exterior, the timepiece received modern GPS-regulated clockworks. The combination gives the historic clock a modern mechanism while preserving the appearance and character that made it a familiar part of Cleveland Street. The result is a restoration that does not simply reproduce an old clock. Instead, it combines original historic materials with modern technology, allowing the landmark to continue serving a practical purpose.A family craftFor Boyd, the project also carries a personal connection to clockmaking. He learned the trade from his father, David N. Boyd Sr., who began repairing clocks when he was 14. David H. Boyd grew up accompanying his father on service calls and helping with the removal of weights and pendulums from grandfather clocks. By the age of 16, he was making house calls himself.The younger Boyd has since spent nearly four decades repairing and restoring timepieces. His approach to the profession is notably practical. In the Cleveland Street Alliance's account, Boyd describes himself less as a horologist than as a mechanic whose speciality happens to be clocks.Back where it belongsAfter months in the workshop, the restored clock was returned to the corner of Cleveland Street and Fort Harrison Avenue. Its public unveiling on July 25 drew more than 3,000 people. For residents and visitors, the return meant more than seeing an old clock repaired. It marked the return of a familiar piece of the city's streetscape. Boyd described historic public clocks as objects that can become part of a community's daily life. People see them repeatedly over many years, eventually associating them with a particular place and period of their lives. That may be the most significant part of this restoration. The clock's value is not limited to its age, its mechanical workings or the 700 hours invested in repairing it. It is also a physical link to Clearwater's past. After surviving nearly a century outdoors, the 95-year-old hands and original dial are once again above Cleveland Street, keeping time for another generation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump-backed Freedom Fuel chain faces lawsuit over $4 million unpaid gas bill
articles.summary: US News: A fuel supplier has sued a company that purchased gasoline for Freedom Fuel Network, alleging it failed to pay about $4 million for fuel delivered to .
articles.body: A fuel supplier has sued a company that purchased gasoline for Freedom Fuel Network, alleging it failed to pay about $4 million for fuel delivered to the discount gas station chain in July.Freedom Fuel had drawn attention after US President Donald Trump praised the chain in July for selling gasoline at significantly lower prices than competing stations in the Philadelphia area. Trump said the company was “taking the lead, and others should follow” in a Truth Social post.The lawsuit was filed on August 19 in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania by Mansfield Oil Company of Gainesville, Georgia. It alleges that KRSM, the company that purchased the fuel for Freedom Fuel, has not paid for gasoline deliveries made to at least 10 Freedom Fuel stations.According to Mansfield Oil’s attorney, Urs Broderick Furrer, at least 1.12 million gallons of gasoline were delivered to the stations. “Despite the fact that the last delivery was more than five weeks ago, KRSM has not paid one dollar towards the $4,000,000 that KRSM owes Mansfield,” Furrer told CNN in an email.The lawsuit names KRSM and its president, Syed Kazmi, as defendants but does not name Freedom Fuel Network. The suit describes KRSM as a foreign corporation with its principal business address in Lawrenceville, New Jersey.KRSM’s attorney, Mauro Tucci, disputed the allegations and said the company intends to contest the case. He described it as “an accounting dispute over fuel invoices mis-priced by Mansfield Oil.”Freedom Fuel drew attention in July after its stations began selling gasoline for about $3.48 a gallon around the July 4 holiday weekend, compared with a Pennsylvania average of $3.99 at the time. The chain had 25 rebranded stations then and has since added four more, according to its website.Trump also said in his July 1 post that gas prices would return to the record-low levels Americans had seen before the US military operation in Iran. However, the national average remained at $4.08 a gallon on Monday, according to AAA, while Pennsylvania's average stood at $4.22.Freedom Fuel’s prices have also risen, with several stations in the Philadelphia suburbs listed by GasBuddy at about $3.99 a gallon.The White House has denied any connection between the Trump administration and Freedom Fuel, describing it as “a private company with no government support or subsidies”.“The administration is not involved in the company, nor has the administration given the company any funding. There is no other entity or person subsidizing the lower gasoline costs,” a White House spokesperson told CNN. “They are simply reducing their margin to make prices at the pump more affordable for drivers in Philadelphia and New Jersey.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ryan Seacrest sells his 40-acre Napa Valley estate for $18.5 million after asking $22 million, inside the sprawling retreat he bought for $14 million, renovated and listed twice before finding a buyer
articles.summary: Real Estate News: Ryan Seacrest has closed a two-year chapter with his sprawling 40-acre Napa Valley estate, selling it for $18.5 million after asking $22 million. The .
articles.body: Ryan Seacrest has closed a two-year chapter with his sprawling 40-acre Napa Valley estate, selling it for $18.5 million after asking $22 million. The American Idol host first listed the St. Helena estate in the summer of 2024, after a major renovation. It was taken off the market just over a month later. But the estate reappeared in April 2025, again listed at $22 million, according to a report by Realtor website. The asking price was reduced to $18.8 million earlier this year, and finally a buyer came along. The final sale was just $300,000 less than that reduced figure, reports Mansion Global. According to property records, Seacrest bought the estate through an LLC in 2020 for $14 million. So the $18.5 million sale could mean a profit of $4.5 million before taxes, transaction costs and the massive renovation costs. Under Seacrest's ownership, the property was redesigned with the project managed by architectural designer Silvia Nobili of Nobili Marques Arquitectura. The renovation included new finishes, a larger master suite, an additional guest suite and a complete redo of the guest house.10,750 square foot Napa retreatAccording to the report by Realtor, the estate is headed by a 10,750 square foot main house that includes five bedrooms and six bathrooms. The sprawling home features a mix of traditional materials with modern design and plenty of indoor-outdoor living areas. Inside, the property boasts soaring ceilings, reclaimed wood beams, wide-plank oak floors, limestone walls and seven fireplaces. The custom cabinetry, doors and windows, and lighting add to the custom feel. The chef's kitchen is particularly unique, with its own fireplace with rotisserie and pizza oven. Other features of the home include a library gallery, television room, gym, garden room, laundry facilities and storage areas and a three-car garage. The master suite was expanded in the renovation and features a private office, terrace and outdoor spa garden.Resort-style amenities in natural surroundingsThe estate has a lot of outdoor space which is a plus. The grounds include an infinity-edge pool and spa, a central courtyard set up for large-scale entertaining, many terraces and a bocce court. Seacrest also planted 220 fruiting Italian olive trees that form a private grove across the property. Mature trees and native plantings contribute to the sense of seclusion. Large pocketing doors open the interiors directly onto the terraces and surrounding landscape, reinforcing the estate’s indoor-outdoor design. The property also has security and surveillance systems, built-in audio, a Lutron lighting system and a whole-property backup generator.A home created for privacy and viewsFrom the property, Seacrest enjoyed one of his favorite features, a panoramic view across the Napa Valley. The secluded setting was filled with greenery and an atmosphere of peace and hot-air balloons could be seen in the distance occasionally. Minutes from the Meadowood Resort and downtown St. Helena, the estate provides the next owner easy access to restaurants, resorts and Napa Valley attractions while still maintaining a strong sense of privacy. The new owner has not been identified. But for Seacrest, the sale marks the end of an ambitious real estate project that turned a $14 million purchase into a $18.5 million sale after several years of ownership, renovation and two separate efforts to find a buyer.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Anwick chicken droppings gas plant proposal to be decided
articles.summary: Lincolnshire County Council will rule on the plans for Anwick at a meeting next week.
articles.body:
An application to build a biogas plant fuelled by chicken droppings will be decided next week.

If approved, the site on the outskirts of Anwick, near Sleaford, Lincolnshire, would process 120,000 tonnes of faeces and feedstock waste to produce gas pumped into the National Grid.

An action group that has previously said it would "kill the village" has set up a petition signed by more than 600 people, but developer Stream Bioenergy said the project would be "a state-of-the-art development with a robust multi-stage odour control system".

The plans went before Lincolnshire County Council's planning committee in May, but they were withdrawn before a final decision was made.

The proposed plant would include eight digester tanks which are 25m (82ft) tall, as well as a processing building, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

Villagers fear if the plans were to go ahead it would lead to bad smells and heavy traffic in the area.

In May, Stream Bioenergy said: "We and the Lincolnshire County Council planning department agreed to defer this application from the May planning committee agenda to allow us appropriate time to fully review the planning officer's report before presenting at a future planning committee.

"We remain fully committed to this development, which represents a £115m investment that will support the important agri-food sector in Lincolnshire."

The report by council officers said the size of the development would lead to "the industrialisation of the countryside with significant adverse harm to the landscape character".

The application will be determined at a meeting on 7 September.

articles.title: Dungannon: Boy, 16, appears in court charged with murder and attempted murder
articles.summary: Sidi Djalo, who was 61, was found alongside his injured eight-year-old daughter at a house in Dungannon on Saturday morning.
articles.body:
A teenage boy has appeared in court charged with the murder of a man in Dungannon, County Tyrone, and the attempted murder of two other people in the same incident.

The body of the Sidi Djalo, who was 61, was found alongside his injured eight-year-old daughter at a house on Lisnahull Road on Saturday morning.

The man's 48-year-old wife sustained non-life threatening injuries during the attack.

The 16-year-old defendant, who cannot be named because of his age, was also charged with making threats to kill. He appeared in court in Omagh on Tuesday morning and was remanded in custody.

The teenager spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address.

BBC News NI understands the man who died was from Guinea-Bissau, but had lived in Northern Ireland for more than two decades.

During the hearing, defence solicitor Jarlath Faloon said there were "clear concerns" about the defendant's mental health.

Faloon said the defendant had been examined by a mental health nurse over the weekend but not at psychiatric level.

The judge made an order to conduct a mental health assessment of the defendant.

He is due to appear on 15 September at Dungannon Youth Court.

articles.title: Overnight A31 road closures for further wildfire repairs
articles.summary: The A31 was closed for two weeks following the devastating wildfire in the New Forest in August.
articles.body:
A dual carriageway that was closed for nearly two weeks due to a wildfire is to shut overnight for further repair work over two weeks.

A major incident was declared after a van fire on the A31 in the New Forest near Ringwood, Hampshire, on 9 August went on to destroy about 0.6 sq miles (1.6 sq km) of heathland .

The road reopened on 22 August but overnight closures will be put in place until 11 September for work to replace the safety barrier along both carriageways and remove any further trees damaged by the fire.

During the overnight closures - between 21:00 and 06:00 - the westbound carriageway at Stoney Cross will also be resurfaced.

The A31 will be closed between M27 junction 2 and Ringwood.

Eastbound traffic is being diverted via Fordingbridge and Salisbury while westbound traffic faces a detour via Lyndhurst and Christchurch.

Before the road reopened, work was carried out to replace 2,624ft (800m) of safety barriers and 4,921ft (1,500m) of boundary fencing.

Temporary speed limits will remain in place when the road is open during the day.

National Highways previously described the repair work as "substantial and the conditions challenging".

Damaged fencing had to be replaced to stop animals getting on to the A31 before the road could be safely reopened.

The closure of the A31, the main route between Bournemouth and Southampton, caused severe congestion as traffic was diverted through New Forest villages and businesses and tourist attractions reported drops in income .

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial: No verdict after 17 hours of jury deliberations; hearing to continue Tuesday
articles.summary: US News: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial spent a third day deliberating without reaching a verdict, bringing their total deliberation time to about 17 hours.
articles.body: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial spent a third day deliberating without reaching a verdict, bringing their total deliberation time to about 17 hours. The jury, which is deciding whether the former labour and delivery nurse was criminally responsible for killing her three children in 2023, is set to continue deliberations on Tuesday.According to The Associated Press (AP), jurors began deliberating Thursday after hearing testimony from more than 70 prosecution witnesses and 10 defence witnesses during a five-week trial. The case has drawn attention to maternal mental health and postpartum psychosis.Clancy, 36, does not deny strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight-month-old Callan — with exercise bands at the family's home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on January 24, 2023. She then attempted suicide while her husband was away getting takeout and going to a pharmacy.Her defence has argued that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis and had lost touch with reality when she killed the children. Clancy had sought treatment for her worsening mental health in the months before the killings and was discharged from a psychiatric hospital less than three weeks before the deaths.Prosecutors have argued that Clancy knew what she was doing and deliberately killed the children before attempting suicide. They said she was depressed and overwhelmed by caring for the children and wanted to end her life while taking them with her.Medical experts called by both sides disagreed over Clancy's state of mind at the time of the killings. Clancy did not testify during the trial.The jury could find her guilty of murder or the lesser charge of manslaughter, or acquit her if it determines that she was not criminally responsible because of her psychiatric condition.If convicted, she could face life in prison, while an acquittal on mental health grounds could lead to her release or confinement in a psychiatric facility.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How conviction of Duane Davis could help inspire efforts to find killer of Notorious B.I.G.
articles.summary: The murder of Notorious B.I.G. was thought to be linked to the killing of his rival Tupac Shakur and it came up a lot in the trial.
articles.body:
The conviction of Duane "Keffe D" Davis in Las Vegas has brought an end to one of the world's most famous unsolved murder cases.

"We're talking about the greatest rapper of all time, an icon, and not a single arrest or prosecution for 30 years," former prosecutor Neama Rahmani told the BBC of the conviction in rapper Tupac Shakur's murder. "This is huge. It was a tough case. It's a cold case."

It gives closure to 30 years of mystery, the end of an era, he added.

It led to tears from rapper Shakur's family in the courtroom, promises from Davis that he would appeal and curiosity from others looking on as to what it could mean for an almost identical case - the unsolved murder of Notorious B.I.G. or Biggie Smalls, also known by his legal name of Christopher Wallace.

Wallace, a New Yorker, was Shakur's big rival and the two rappers embodied the East Coast - West Coast feud that dominated 1990s hip-hop. Wallace was killed in Los Angeles a few months after Shakur and in near identical circumstances - a drive-by shooting. No one has ever been charged.

It has long been believed the two murders were linked and Wallace's name came up a lot in the Duane Davis trial - he and Davis were at the same party that night and David was interviewed by police after Wallace was killed. The investigator who conducted that interview even testified at the latest trial.

The breakthrough in finally solving the Shakur case largely came down to one thing - Davis' own words.

Through documentaries with the media, his own memoir, podcasts and even a secret police interview - he acknowledged his role in Shakur's death. Davis said he tossed a firearm in the backseat and his nephew, Orlando Anderson, used the gun to fatally shoot Shakur as they pulled up alongside his vehicle in Las Vegas on 7 September, 1996.

Anderson was shot dead in 1998, having denied killing Shakur.

During the trial, there were no eye-witnesses to place Davis as being in the car, no murder weapon presented, no video or photo evidence. His defence team went as far as to argue there wasn't even proof that he was in Las Vegas that night.

Rahmani said it was a difficult case to prosecute. He noted the rumours and speculation surrounding Davis were nothing new and had been around for decades - but the decision to charge him and go to trial was an "uphill climb" - a gutsy move - for prosecutors.

"Look, when you're a prosecutor, you're expected to win every time. They made a difficult decision to charge a case that a lot of people thought might be a loser," he explained. "And they got justice, where other people didn't even bother trying."

Davis' attorney Michael Sanft asked the jury to consider "what facts do you have?" He urged the panel, before they decided their guilty verdict, to discredit his client as a liar who told tales to sell books and make money.

"There's no proof," he argued to the jury.

The moment the guilty verdict was read in court, Shakur's family burst into emotion. Some cried and wiped tears with tissues. Others hugged and held hands - one family member even embraced one of the prosecutors in the case.

Trial attorney Shaun Kent said the case really evolved with each interview and moment that Davis decided to open his mouth and talk about the case more.

"There are no other witnesses, besides him," Kent told the BBC before the trial, noting that the "strongest witness against him - is him".

Rahmani said in his opinion, Davis would "go down as one of the world's dumbest criminals", who likely would have never have faced charges if he had stayed silent.

"He really couldn't stop himself," Rahmani added. "Even when he was arrested and in custody, he was giving interviews."

Much of the Shakur trial forced the jury to place themselves back to the 1990s, at a time of intense gang violence that had infiltrated roots into hip-hop music and rivalries between East-Coast and West-Coast rappers.

It was a time of deep-rooted mistrust in policing and a street code that forbade snitching to authorities.

Even Shakur, after being hit multiple times in the drive-by shooting that would later kill him, refused to talk to authorities. "We'll take care of it," he said in an ambulance as an officer tried to question him on who did it.

The silence was echoed months later in the shooting death of Biggie Smalls.

Biggie, one of the biggest East Coast rappers, was leaving an after-party in Los Angeles for the Soul Train Music Awards, when a black Chevrolet pulled up to his vehicle at a red light and opened fire on 9 March, 1997. It was almost exactly six months after the shooting that killed Shakur, one of the biggest West Coast rappers.

Both were Grammy-nominated artists at the top of their genre, making millions and being played incessantly on the radio. They were also at the centre of a feud between East Coast and West Coast rap, that spilled over into their lyrics and also led to threats and physical violence.

Both shootings led to no arrests, no convictions, just rumours and conspiracies and gang violence that exploded on the streets of Los Angeles as street gangs sought to hold one another accountable in the aftermath of both rappers' deaths.

Like Shakur's death, countless theories and names have surrounded the death of Biggie in Los Angeles, but police with the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) have not made any arrests.

"It's really a stain on the LAPD. The fact that this could happen and not a single arrest was made and no one was prosecuted," Rahmani said, noting Biggie's killing happened on a public street in the middle of the second most populous US city.

"Prosecutors don't like to lose and tend to be a little gun shy," Rahmani explained. "But, maybe this [Tupac's conviction] will embolden folks in Los Angeles to maybe take another look at it, a cold case that's coming up on 30 years."

Asked about the cases and whether the Tupac murder conviction could revive Biggie's death, the LAPD told the BBC that it was aware of the conviction and the investigation into Biggie's case remained active.

"The murder of Christopher Wallace remains an open, unsolved case within LAPD's Robbery-Homicide Division," Lt Elpidio Orozco said, urging anyone with any tips to call authorities.

articles.title: Teen girl charged with murder over recording of San Diego mosque attack
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the 17-year-old from North Carolina also published a manifesto from the two teenage gunmen in the 18 May attack.
articles.body:
A 17-year-old girl has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting after prosecutors say she recorded a livestream of an attack on a San Diego mosque that left three people dead.

Prosecutors say the girl also published a manifesto from two teenage gunmen who carried out the attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego on 18 May.

The teenager, from North Carolina, was arrested last week and indicted by a grand jury on Monday, according to Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill.

Speaking at a news conference, O'Neill said: "The thought of her going back to school, with the weekend approaching, holy days approaching, we didn't know what she was capable of."

The teenager now faces three murder charges and one count of conspiracy. O'Neill explained that under North Carolina law, a person accused of aiding and abetting a crime can be held criminally responsible in the same way as the person who carried it out.

Authorities say the attack was carried out by two males - aged 17 and 18 - who opened fire at the mosque, before taking their own lives.

O'Neill said the pair had two aims that day: "Number one, to kill as many people as possible on that day. Secondly, they wanted this carnage and destruction recorded ... livestreamed."

A security guard at the mosque, Amin Abdullah, exchanged gunfire with the attackers and initiated a lockdown, helping protect around 140 children who were inside the building.

Abdullah and two worshippers - Mansour Kaziha and Nader Awad, who drew the attentions of the shooters in a parking lot - were fatally shot.

San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl previously described Abdullah's actions as "heroic", saying they had "undoubtedly" saved lives.

According to investigators, the shooters recorded the attack using cameras mounted on GoPro-style helmets. O'Neill said the pair had also planned further attacks "at a local Jewish temple and finally at a predominantly African American high school".

Authorities said the teenagers had an arsenal of around 30 guns and a crossbow, which investigators say were taken from one of the shooter's parents.

The attackers also left behind writings containing racist and antisemitic views, as well as references to white supremacist ideologies.

The document, which was reviewed by the BBC's US news partner CBS News, pointed to a gunman who murdered 51 people at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 2019, as one of their models.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Warren Buffett: "Rule No. 1: Never lose money. Rule No. 2: Never..."
articles.summary: US News: Two investors can pursue the exact same market and end up with very different long-term results, not because one picked better winners, but because on.
articles.body: Two investors can pursue the exact same market and end up with very different long-term results, not because one picked better winners, but because one avoided catastrophic losses the other didn't. One chases upside aggressively, accepting large downside risk as the reasonable cost of potentially large returns. The other treats avoiding permanent, irreversible loss as the actual foundation everything else gets built on, understanding that a single severe loss can undo years of otherwise solid gains. Buffett's rule, repeated so often it has become something close to a personal motto, isn't a claim that his investments never fluctuate in value; they clearly do. It's a statement about a specific kind of loss: the permanent, unrecoverable kind that comes from paying too much for something, misjudging a business fundamentally, or taking on risk that can wipe out capital rather than temporarily reduce it.Quote of the day by Warren Buffett"Rule No. 1: Never lose money. Rule No. 2: Never forget Rule No. 1."Written by an investor whose whole method is built around avoiding disasterWhat gives this line extra weight is how closely it matches Buffett's actual documented investment philosophy over more than six decades running Berkshire Hathaway. Trained under Benjamin Graham at Columbia, Buffett built his entire approach around the concept of a "margin of safety," buying businesses and shares only when their price left substantial room for error, specifically so that a mistake in judgment wouldn't translate directly into a devastating loss of capital. That discipline is a large part of why Berkshire avoided the worst of the dot-com bubble in the late 1990s, when Buffett was publicly criticised for missing out on rapidly rising technology stocks he didn't understand well enough to value confidently, a decision that looked overly cautious for a couple of years and then looked prescient once the bubble collapsed.Buffett has also been unusually open, for a public figure of his stature, about his own investment mistakes, including his often-cited regret over ever buying the original Berkshire Hathaway textile business at all, and other specific investments he has publicly acknowledged as errors in his annual shareholder letters. That openness reinforces rather than undermines the rule: the point was never that he avoids all mistakes, but that the mistakes he does make are structured to be survivable rather than catastrophic, precisely because avoiding permanent capital loss was always the first filter applied before any decision about potential upside.A simple way to actually use this ideaThe useful move here is treating downside protection as the first question in any significant decision, not an afterthought considered only after the potential upside has already gotten a person excited. It's easy to evaluate an opportunity almost entirely by how good the best-case outcome looks, while paying only glancing attention to how bad, and how recoverable, the worst-case outcome actually is. This applies well beyond investing. Career moves, major purchases, and personal commitments all carry the same asymmetry, where an appealing upside can quietly crowd out a clear-eyed look at what happens if things go wrong instead.A fair test, before committing meaningfully to any risk, financial or otherwise, is to ask specifically whether a bad outcome would be a setback or something closer to unrecoverable. That question won't eliminate risk from any real decision, and Buffett himself has never claimed it should. It usually clarifies which risks are actually worth taking and which ones only look reasonable because their worst-case outcome hasn't been examined closely enough yet, which is precisely the gap his rule is designed to close before it becomes expensive.Other famous quotes by Warren Buffett"Price is what you pay. Value is what you get." "Be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful." "It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2024, Hurricane Helene lifted a concrete Virginia bridge off its foundation and pushed it to the shoreline; after $195.5 million in regional repairs, its replacement opens today
articles.summary: US News: Another milestone in a major Hurricane Helene recovery project in Southwest Virginia, as the replacement Route 1212 bridge opens to traffic in Damascu.
articles.body: Another milestone in a major Hurricane Helene recovery project in Southwest Virginia, as the replacement Route 1212 bridge opens to traffic in Damascus on September 1. According to reports, the bridge across Laurel Creek was one of hundreds of transportation structures damaged in the powerful storm that hit the region in September 2024. Drivers on the new bridge, which is now finished, are being told to be careful while work continues to finish off around the site, states an online report by the Virginia Department of Transportation. It has been reported that Hurricane Helene left more than 500 sites needing repair at an estimated cost of $195.5 million across the Bristol District in a huge cleanup and rebuilding job. The damage included 394 structures including bridges and culverts. The storm did so much damage that five bridges needed to be completely replaced, a testament to the incredible force of the flooding and winds that ripped through Southwest Virginia. One such structure was the Route 1212 bridge in Damascus. The old bridge was damaged on a local level as well. The power of the storm ripped the concrete structure from its foundation and toward the shore of Laurel Creek.A bridge powered by the force of the stormThe destruction was unusual, and showed the extreme power of Hurricane Helene. The movement of the bridge was a demonstration of how floodwaters and the strength of the storm can overcome even the strongest infrastructure. Transportation officials have said the incident is a particularly vivid example of the damage Helene has dealt across the region. The replacement project was part of an effort to restore transportation connections and repair storm-damaged infrastructure.Hundreds of buildings needed to be repairedThe 394 affected structures included bridges and culverts, as well as sites requiring erosion repairs, debris removal and other structural rehabilitation. In the end five bridges needed complete replacement. Crews also replaced the Route 859 bridge at Konnarock in Washington County, the Route 725 bridge at Taylors Valley in Washington County, the Route 847 bridge in Grayson County and the Route 800, or St. Clair Creek Road, bridge in Smyth County, in addition to the Route 1212 bridge in Damascus. The recovery operation also included the replacement of four culverts.Recovery continues throughout Southwest VirginiaWith the opening of the Route 1212 replacement, all Hurricane Helene repair and replacement projects are complete in the Bristol District. The new bridge restores a key local transportation link, but crews will remain in the area to complete work at the site. Motorists are therefore advised to exercise caution and be on the lookout for construction personnel and equipment. Reopening is also a big step in recovering from one of the most destructive recent storms in Southwest Virginia. A year after Helene swept through the area, the Route 1212 bridge is a lasting reminder of the storm's extraordinary power and the scale of the infrastructure effort needed to rebuild.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
