articles.title: This Texas basin was once dismissed as a ‘graveyard’. Now its oil economy supports 853,924 jobs and generates billions in economic activity across the US
articles.summary: US News: A century ago, the Permian Basin was hardly the place anyone would have picked as an engine of the American economy. Early observers were so unimpress.
articles.body: A century ago, the Permian Basin was hardly the place anyone would have picked as an engine of the American economy. Early observers were so unimpressed by parts of the landscape that the region was dismissed as a “graveyard” according to WorldOil. Today, the same stretch of West Texas and southeastern New Mexico sits at the centre of one of the country’s most important energy-producing regions. Its impact now reaches far beyond oil wells and drilling rigs.According to Permian Basin Petroleum Association (PBPA) 2024 report, the basin’s nationwide employment impact at 853,924 jobs, while activity connected to it generated about $18.2 billion in taxes for Texas and New Mexico. Roads, schools, hospitals, universities, suppliers and local businesses all sit within the economic chain created by the basin. And with projections pointing towards an even larger role by 2050, the Permian’s transformation is no longer just an oil story.How one US oil basin became a lifeline for communities across two statesThe 2024 report figures put the Permian Basin's nationwide employment impact at 853,924 jobs. These positions are not limited to workers directly involved in drilling and production. The wider economic activity associated with the basin supports businesses, public revenues and services in communities connected to the energy industry.During the year covered by the report, activity linked to the basin generated about $18.2 billion in taxes across Texas and New Mexico. That money reaches parts of everyday public life that can seem distant from an oil well, including schools, roads, emergency services, hospitals and universities.Energy production is not simply a separate industrial activity in the region; it is woven into the finances of communities on both sides of the state line.How a relatively small region became an economic powerhouseThe basin occupies only a relatively small share of the populations of the two states, yet its economic footprint is considerably larger.According to PBPA, in New Mexico, the Permian region accounts for 25.9% of private-sector gross domestic product while representing 9.2% of the state's population. The contrast is also visible in Texas. There, the basin accounts for 8.1% of private-sector GDP despite containing just 1.6% of the state's population.The financial contribution reaches higher education and public institutions, too. According to the report, $3.6 billion went to Texas' Permanent University Fund and Permanent School Fund combined. Those funds provide a long-standing connection between energy activity and public education in the state.A resource giant that could supply half of America’s oil by 2030The scale of the resource beneath the basin remains a central part of the picture. The report estimates that the Permian contains 92.7 billion barrels of recoverable oil and about 211 trillion cubic feet of recoverable natural gas.That makes the basin significant not only for the states where it is located but also for the wider US energy system. Its production has grown into a major component of domestic oil supply, with the report projecting that the region could account for half of US oil production by 2030.The scale is large enough to put the basin in an unusual global position. If it were treated as an independent country, its oil output would place it among the world's five largest producers.How solar and wind are changing the Permian BasinEnergy development in the Permian is also taking place alongside expansion in renewable power. New Mexico was expected to increase its solar capacity by an estimated 115% in 2024, according to the report, while Texas was projected to record 76% growth.Wind and solar projects have been expanding around the basin as companies and communities add other forms of generation to an area long associated with oil and natural gas. The coexistence of these industries has become another part of the region's changing energy landscape.The report also places the Permian relatively low in carbon dioxide emissions per barrel of oil equivalent when compared with other major onshore producing basins around the world. Its ranking was described as second lowest among those major basins.Why the Permian needs more roads, schools and public servicesRapid industrial activity creates its own demands. Roads, utilities, schools, hospitals and other public infrastructure all have to accommodate communities where employment and investment can shift with the energy sector.That is why infrastructure spending features prominently in discussions about the Permian's economic future. The region's energy companies and public authorities have an interest in keeping transport networks and essential services capable of supporting continued activity.Don Evans, chairman of the Permian Strategic Partnership, said, “The Permian Basin provides indispensable resources to energy security, making significant contributions to our nation’s robust economy every year.”How big could the Permian Basin become by 2050The economic projections attached to the basin extend well beyond the current production cycle. The Permian Strategic Partnership's report estimates that the region could generate roughly $350 billion in gross product and support around 1.2 million jobs nationally by 2050.Those numbers are projections rather than guarantees, and they depend on future production, investment, energy demand and infrastructure development. Still, they illustrate the scale that the basin's economic role could reach if its expansion continues.For Texas and New Mexico, the stakes are particularly direct. Their public finances and private economies already benefit from the activity generated around the basin, while companies operating there remain important to the national energy supply.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Six years overdue, Army begins first full overhaul of  indigenous Arjun tanks
articles.summary: News News: Six years behind schedule, the Army has finally kicked off the rebuild of its Arjun tanks, with two Mk-1s set to be stripped down and refurbished at t.
articles.body: Six years behind schedule, the Army has finally kicked off the rebuild of its Arjun tanks, with two Mk-1s set to be stripped down and refurbished at the Heavy Vehicles Factory in Avadi. The two tanks will also get 26 upgrades borrowed from the newer Mk-1A variant and will serve as a pilot for the overhaul of the Army's remaining 124-strong fleet. The repair procedures developed here will form the template going forward.The Arjun has never had a full overhaul before. A 2016 CAG report flagged that the tank, inducted from 2004, was due for its first overhaul by 2020, but no agency had even been identified to carry it out. The same audit found the Arjun sitting idle since 2013 due to a lack of repair facilities and poor spares support from HVF. Engine-level work continued separately, with Engine Factory Avadi and CVRDE running a powerpack overhaul exercise that the current project now builds on, but a full hull-and-turret rebuild is happening for the first time.Of the 26 upgrades, six are major, including a commander's panoramic sight, the Mk-II gunner's sight, an automatic target tracker, an improved muzzle reference system, upgraded tracks and a better running gear system. The remaining 20 are smaller fixes, ranging from an auxiliary power unit and improved fire suppression to LED headlamps and better dust sealing.The Arjun Mk-1A programme remains stalled as the 118 tanks ordered from the Heavy Vehicles Factory in 2021 for Rs 7,523 crore are yet to be delivered, with engine supply emerging as the principal bottleneck. Conceived as a major upgrade over the Mk-1, the Mk-1A variant was designed to sharpen firepower, mobility and survivability. It carries a redesigned turret with improved Kanchan armour and explosive reactive armour, while introducing 89 enhancements, 73 of which could be retrofitted into the earlier Mk-1. Standout additions include non-explosive reactive armour, integration of the gun-launched SAMHO anti-tank guided missile, automatic target tracking, a new commander's panoramic sight, and uncooled thermal imaging systems for both gunner and driver.Crew safety has been bolstered with containerised ammunition bins, while agility is improved through a redesigned suspension and advanced running gear. With higher indigenous content, the Mk-1A reflects India's push for self-reliance, though delivery delays underline persistent challenges in defence production. The existing fleet of 124 Mk-1s, inducted between 2004 and 2010, equips two armoured regiments: the 43 Armoured Regiment and the 75 Armoured Regiment.
